Read About Cappadocia

A landscape two volcanoes built and a thousand years of hidden lives carved into it.

A Region Built by Two Volcanoes

Almost everything a visitor sees in Cappadocia — the cones of Uçhisar and Ortahisar, the soft ridgelines of Love Valley, the pale walls of Göreme's monastery — is the same material: volcanic ash and lava laid down over millions of years by two now-dormant volcanoes, Erciyes and Hasan Dağ, which still stand on the horizon in most directions. The ash compacted into a soft rock called tuff, and centuries of wind and flash floods carved it into cones, columns, and ravines. Harder caps of basalt on top of some columns eroded more slowly than the tuff beneath them, which is why so many fairy chimneys end in a dark, mushroom-like cap balanced over a narrower stalk.

The rock's softness is the region's second defining fact, after its shape. Tuff can be cut with hand tools, which meant that for as long as people have lived here, they have not built houses so much as excavated them.

Refuge Underground

The earliest tunnels beneath Cappadocia may predate the Byzantine era, but it was Christian communities fleeing Roman, and later Arab, persecution who expanded them into the vast underground cities this guide's second day visits. Derinkuyu alone descends some eighteen levels and could reportedly shelter thousands of people along with their livestock and grain stores for weeks at a time, sealed behind massive rolling stone doors that could only be opened from inside. Ventilation shafts, wells, wine presses, and even a school room have been identified in its passages.

The same soft rock that let monks carve a hundred churches into Ihlara's canyon walls is the rock a visitor now sleeps inside, a few doors down from where this trip's hotel keeps its own dining room.

Above ground, the same instinct produced the rock-cut churches of Göreme and Ihlara: hundreds of chapels carved directly into cliffs and cones, many still holding frescoes painted by monks who lived, worshipped, and were eventually buried inside the rock they had shaped. The tradition never really ended — it simply moved into hospitality. The cave hotel rooms booked for a trip like this one are dug by the same method the Byzantine monks used, with electricity and plumbing added afterward.

Why the Balloons Fly Here

Cappadocia is one of a small handful of places on Earth where hot air ballooning runs on most mornings of the year, and that too traces back to the volcanic terrain. The region's valleys sit inside a natural bowl of high plateau, which traps unusually still air at dawn before the day's wind picks up. That predictable calm window — rare enough that many flatter landscapes elsewhere cannot support commercial ballooning at all — is what allows a hundred or more balloons to launch together most clear mornings, drifting low over the same fairy chimneys the underground-city builders once quarried from below.

A Living Wine Country

The volcanic soil that shaped the landscape also shapes what grows in it. Cappadocia has produced wine for thousands of years — vine cultivation here is often traced back to the Hittites — using native grape varieties such as Emir, Narince, and Kalecik Karası that are rarely found outside central Turkey. Wineries around Ürgüp still age some of their wine in cellars cut into the same tuff as the region's oldest churches, and the volcanic minerals in the soil are often credited with giving the local wine its distinct, faintly smoky character.
